chunks.locator: The story in one minute · lines 5–9
chunks.text:
## The story in one minute
ShopEase is an online shopping service. Customers browse, pay and place orders. Gaurav keeps releases, monitoring and recovery organised. He is due to leave on 25 November 2026. Savinay is preparing to take over, and Rudransh coordinates the review.

This is an authored, fictional DevOps case study for demonstrating INHERIA. Wipro is used only as an illustrative employer in the story; these are not Wipro records, client data or proof of anyone's employment. Incident timelines, decisions and source dates belong to the scenario. No cloud operations, restore tests or human approvals are claimed to have happened.

## Where to start in the live application
1. Select ShopEase - DevOps Case Study in the Active project selector.
2. Open Connected sources. Read this file, document 05 and document 32.
3. Open Project memory. Select a responsibility and inspect its exact source excerpt.
4. Open Investigation. Compare the findings with the 15 priority questions in document 32.
5. Open Continuity risk. Inspect the hypothetical Gaurav-unavailable scenario.
6. Open Handover workspace. The planned Gaurav-to-Savinay transition is ready for review steps, not already approved.
7. Use documents 29-31 to understand what Savinay must demonstrate before closure.

chunks.locator: How to read a status · lines 19–22
chunks.text:
## How to read a status
Pending means a source has been read but an authorised person still needs to verify it. Verified means a reviewer has checked the claim against its evidence. Accepted means the incoming owner personally agreed to a responsibility. A completed exercise needs an actual submission and assessment.
Source status such as "resolved" describes the incident narrative. It does not mark an INHERIA claim verified or prove a real operational test passed.

## What still needs review
Deployment guidance conflicts, backup restoration is unproven, payment reconciliation ownership is unclear, staging access is pending and critical operations have no confirmed backup. These conditions make the review meaningful. Finding a gap does not fix it.

chunks.locator: Releases and environments · lines 5–11
chunks.text:
## Releases and environments
- Staging: a separate place for approved tests, without real customer traffic.
- Production: the system customers use. A practice exercise must not target it.
- Pipeline: the automated sequence that builds, checks and packages a release.
- Artifact: the exact built application package. A digest identifies the package; a mutable tag alone is not enough evidence.
- Health check: a narrow signal that a process responds. It does not prove checkout, payment and order creation work together.

chunks.locator: Recovery words that mean different things · lines 12–19
chunks.text:
## Recovery words that mean different things
- Rollback: returning application code to an earlier release, only when data and interfaces remain compatible.
- Restore: recovering data from a backup into an approved target. It can lose changes after the recovery point.
- Service recovery: coordinating application, data, network and external dependencies until service is usable again.
- RTO: the agreed recovery-time target. ShopEase has no approved target in this pack.
- RPO: the agreed maximum tolerable data-loss interval. ShopEase has no approved target in this pack.
- Idempotency: safely handling a repeated request without charging or fulfilling twice.

chunks.locator: People and evidence · lines 20–27
chunks.text:
## People and evidence
- Primary owner: accountable for organising a responsibility, not necessarily the only person who performs every step.
- Backup owner: someone with agreed scope, access and practical readiness to cover it.
- Escalation: involving the correct authorised team when risk or uncertainty exceeds your remit.
- Evidence: a particular source version and excerpt supporting a claim. A source can still be old or wrong.
- Knowledge gap: a question the available material does not answer adequately.
- Pending review: not approved yet. Lack of evidence is not evidence of success.

chunks.locator: Secret handling · lines 27–28
chunks.text:
## Secret handling
Record the approved secret-manager location and request route, never the value. INHERIA does not grant cloud permissions, rotate credentials or offboard accounts. Access removal remains a separate company process after knowledge-transfer review.

chunks.locator: Common misunderstanding · lines 28–29
chunks.text:
## Common misunderstanding
"The backup job was green" means a job reported success; it does not show the data can be restored. "The pipeline was green" means its configured steps passed; it does not show every customer journey is healthy. "Savinay was assigned" does not mean Savinay accepted.

## Architecture: ShopEase customer journey
System: ShopEase
Status: current draft
Customers reach the Web storefront, which calls the API service. The API writes orders to PostgreSQL and sends payment requests to Payment provider. chunks.locator: Who does what · lines 5–9
chunks.text:
## Who does what
Gaurav is the departing DevOps engineer in the story. His existing INHERIA account remains the organisation administrator; adding the case study does not change that account role.
Savinay is the incoming engineer. He reviews sources, submits practical evidence and personally accepts or rejects transfers.
Rudransh is the handover coordinator with the application's manager role. He coordinates review and closure. He is not a newly created organisation administrator and cannot substitute for technical expertise.

chunks.locator: Supporting teams · lines 10–13
chunks.text:
## Supporting teams
Database team is accountable for schema design, data integrity and approval of destructive data operations. Application team is accountable for business logic, payment idempotency and order reconciliation. Security team is accountable for access policy and incident classification. Client operations is accountable for customer-impact decisions and approved service commitments.
These are scenario teams, not added user accounts. A named, authorised reviewer from each relevant team is still needed.

chunks.locator: Review versus acceptance · lines 14–16
chunks.text:
## Review versus acceptance
Rudransh can check that a source supports a case-study claim; he must request a qualified reviewer for operational correctness. Savinay's proposed assignment does not prove he is ready. Gaurav's notes remain authored drafts until an actual person reviews or confirms them.

chunks.locator: Two-week transfer plan · lines 17–23
chunks.text:
## Two-week transfer plan
Days 1-2: inventory, access requests and missing evidence.
Days 3-5: review deployment, rollback, monitoring and open incidents.
Days 6-8: supervised staging exercises, only after permission and environment checks.
Days 9-11: recovery discussion, corrections and reassessment.
Days 12-14: acceptance of ready responsibilities, explicit handling of blockers and closure review.
Dates are planning targets, not attendance or completion records.

## Procedure: Deployment pipeline - current release walkthrough
Owner: Gaurav
System: Deployment pipeline
Status: draft
Meaning: move one approved package through checks to a known environment.
1. Confirm change reference, environment, qualified release approver and planned window.
2. Inspect the selected commit, test results, image digest and migration notes in the authorised repository.
3. Confirm staging smoke-test evidence for that exact package and configuration.
4. Check rollback compatibility, alert coverage and available escalation owners.
5. Request the approved release through the company workflow. This document and INHERIA do not execute it.
6. After an authorised release, compare task health, errors, checkout and order results with the baseline.
Stop if target, approval, migration compatibility or rollback path is unknown.
Missing: actual workflow export, approval identity and a recent release record.
Sources: document 08; ADR-01/ADR-02 in document 17; incident INC-01 in document 18.
Next action: TASK-01 and TASK-02. Review the disagreement with the old guide before marking this current.

chunks.locator: Reading a failure · lines 21–22

## Reading a failure
Build failure: inspect dependency or compilation output before packaging. Test failure: preserve the failing case. Package publishing failure: check permitted registry access without copying credentials. Deployment failure: distinguish scheduling, configuration and app health. Post-release failure: a green workflow does not override customer symptoms.

## Procedure: Release rollback - compatibility decision and safe boundary
Owner: Gaurav
System: Release rollback
Status: draft
Meaning: use a previous application package only when data and interfaces still support it.
1. Preserve the failing release evidence and identify the last known working artifact.
2. Check schema changes, event format, payment side effects and configuration compatibility.
3. Ask the database/application reviewer to confirm whether rollback is possible or a forward fix is safer.
4. Obtain the incident/release approval in the external operating process.
5. If an authorised operator performs rollback, repeat technical and customer-journey checks and record the result.
Stop if a destructive migration ran, compatibility is unknown or payment effects could be duplicated.
Missing: approved migration compatibility matrix and rollback exercise evidence. This outline is not an approved executable runbook.
Sources: document 10, INC-01, ADR-03. Next action: TASK-03 and TASK-10.
Escalation: database team for data, application team for side effects, incident lead for client impact.

chunks.locator: Why rollback is not database restore · lines 20–21
chunks.text:
## Why rollback is not database restore
Returning an image does not recover deleted data. Restoring a database can discard later orders and needs separate recovery authorisation. Payment transactions may already exist outside ShopEase and must be reconciled separately. Never promise that a single button undoes everything.

chunks.locator: Procedure: PostgreSQL - classify a migration before release · lines 5–15
chunks.text:
## Procedure: PostgreSQL - classify a migration before release
Owner: Gaurav
System: PostgreSQL
Status: draft
Ask the database owner whether a migration is additive, rewrites data, changes constraints or removes fields. Check expected locks, duration, backward compatibility and interrupted-run behaviour.
For a simple additive change, still request staging evidence and application compatibility review. For a destructive change, require a reviewed recovery plan and approval before release.
DevOps coordinates timing and evidence; the database team owns schema/data correctness. Do not infer approval from the existence of a migration file.
Missing: current migration inventory, representative staging rehearsal and named database reviewer.
Sources: ADR-03, INC-03 and document 09. Next action: TASK-10 and TASK-11.
Escalation: database lead; stop on unknown locks, irreversible effects or missing recovery evidence.

chunks.locator: Practical review example · lines 16–17
chunks.text:
## Practical review example
A release renames an order column and removes the old field. The previous application image may still request the old field. Savinay should identify the incompatibility and ask for a supported migration plan, not simply run the older image.

chunks.locator: Avoid misleading dashboards · lines 17–18
chunks.text:
## Avoid misleading dashboards
A quiet dashboard may mean healthy service, missing traffic or failed telemetry. An acknowledged alert does not mean the fault was fixed. A recurring suppressed alert needs an owner, expiry and permanent-fix task; it must not disappear from the handover.

chunks.locator: Procedure: Incident response - triage and escalation · lines 5–19
chunks.text:
## Procedure: Incident response - triage and escalation
Owner: Gaurav
System: Incident response
Status: draft
1. Establish impact: affected customer journey, environment, first symptom and whether an incident lead is active.
2. Check current incident notes, recent release, service status and relevant logs using authorised read access.
3. Separate observations from hypotheses. Preserve timestamps and correlation references without personal data.
4. Compare the observed symptom with incidents 18-25. Similar symptoms do not prove the same cause.
5. Escalate to the component owner and agree the next safe diagnostic step.
6. Track mitigation, recovery checks, communication and follow-up work separately.
Stop if a suggested action changes production without approval, destroys evidence or could repeat a payment.
Missing: current on-call rota and approved severity/communications policy.
Sources: documents 18-25 and 27. Next action: TASK-08 and TASK-13.
Escalation: Rudransh coordinates; technical decisions belong to the qualified responder.

chunks.locator: Minimal incident note · lines 20–21
chunks.text:
## Minimal incident note
Record symptom, start time, impact, observed evidence, actions actually performed, actor, approval reference, result, next check and owner. A workaround stays visible until a permanent fix has evidence. Use "unknown" where information is missing.

# Readiness and closure checklist

ShopEase DevOps case study | Document 31 | Scenario source date: 2026-11-11

chunks.locator: Review each gate · lines 5–13
chunks.text:
## Review each gate
Evidence reviewed: relevant source versions support each approved claim; source origin and uncertainty stay visible.
Ownership confirmed: each responsibility has a verified accountable owner and an explicit transfer assignment.
Incoming acceptance: Savinay personally accepts or rejects each assigned responsibility with reasons.
Practical readiness: required exercises have real submissions and qualified assessment. Planning alone does not prove a restore can run.
Access: required permissions are approved and verified through the company process.
Remaining work: critical gaps have owners, next actions and a recorded disposition; naming an owner alone does not remove the risk.
Closure: the app's closure checks pass and an authorised coordinator reviews the result.

chunks.locator: Honest metric definitions · lines 14–21
chunks.text:
## Honest metric definitions
Evidence coverage is the fraction of visible claims with accessible supporting evidence. It is not a truth or accuracy score.
Verification progress is verified visible claims divided by eligible visible claims. Pending claims must remain in the denominator used by the app.
Responsibility acceptance is accepted transfers divided by created transfers; zero assignments is not 100% completion.
Exercise completion requires assessed work; unstarted, blocked and needs-revision states are not passes.
Stale-source signals indicate age beyond a review interval, not automatic invalidity.
Use the live application's displayed definitions and counts. This document supplies no fabricated percentages.

chunks.locator: Reasons closure should remain blocked · lines 22–24
chunks.text:
## Reasons closure should remain blocked
Missing restore evidence, unknown reconciliation owner, a rejected responsibility, an inaccessible required source, changed evidence requiring re-review or an unassessed exercise can prevent completion. Correct the underlying issue and repeat review; do not bypass the gate for a presentation.
Source: documents 05, 26, 30 and 33. Next action: TASK-24.

System: Deployment pipeline
Status: draft
Before: confirm target, approval, exact artifact, staging evidence, open incidents, database change classification and support coverage.
During: preserve release reference and observations through the approved deployment tool. Stop if unexplained configuration drift or a wrong environment appears.
After: check service health, error rate, latency and one approved test journey. A production check must use the client's approved method; never create an unapproved real charge.
Compare: payment response, recorded order state and relevant correlation identifiers. Do not paste customer information into the handover.
Missing: agreed numeric thresholds, observation window and authorised production test method.
Impact: declaring success too early can hide failed orders.
Sources: documents 06 and 19; ADR-05 in document 17.
Next action: TASK-09; attach an actual observation record when an approved exercise happens.
Escalation: application owner for checkout logic, database owner for integrity, Rudransh for coordination.

## Procedure: Release rollback - compatibility decision and safe boundary
Owner: Gaurav
System: Release rollback
Status: draft
Meaning: use a previous application package only when data and interfaces still support it.
1. Preserve the failing release evidence and identify the last known working artifact.
2. Check schema changes, event format, payment side effects and configuration compatibility.
3. Ask the database/application reviewer to confirm whether rollback is possible or a forward fix is safer.
4. Obtain the incident/release approval in the external operating process.
5. If an authorised operator performs rollback, repeat technical and customer-journey checks and record the result.
Stop if a destructive migration ran, compatibility is unknown or payment effects could be duplicated.
Missing: approved migration compatibility matrix and rollback exercise evidence. This outline is not an approved executable runbook.
Sources: document 10, INC-01, ADR-03. Next action: TASK-03 and TASK-10.
Escalation: database team for data, application team for side effects, incident lead for client impact.

## Procedure: PostgreSQL - classify a migration before release
Owner: Gaurav
System: PostgreSQL
Status: draft
Ask the database owner whether a migration is additive, rewrites data, changes constraints or removes fields. Check expected locks, duration, backward compatibility and interrupted-run behaviour.
For a simple additive change, still request staging evidence and application compatibility review. For a destructive change, require a reviewed recovery plan and approval before release.
DevOps coordinates timing and evidence; the database team owns schema/data correctness. Do not infer approval from the existence of a migration file.
Missing: current migration inventory, representative staging rehearsal and named database reviewer.
Sources: ADR-03, INC-03 and document 09. Next action: TASK-10 and TASK-11.
Escalation: database lead; stop on unknown locks, irreversible effects or missing recovery evidence.

## Procedure: Incident response - triage and escalation
Owner: Gaurav
System: Incident response
Status: draft
1. Establish impact: affected customer journey, environment, first symptom and whether an incident lead is active.
2. Check current incident notes, recent release, service status and relevant logs using authorised read access.
3. Separate observations from hypotheses. Preserve timestamps and correlation references without personal data.
4. Compare the observed symptom with incidents 18-25. Similar symptoms do not prove the same cause.
5. Escalate to the component owner and agree the next safe diagnostic step.
6. Track mitigation, recovery checks, communication and follow-up work separately.
Stop if a suggested action changes production without approval, destroys evidence or could repeat a payment.
Missing: current on-call rota and approved severity/communications policy.
Sources: documents 18-25 and 27. Next action: TASK-08 and TASK-13.
Escalation: Rudransh coordinates; technical decisions belong to the qualified responder.

## Procedure: PostgreSQL recovery - inspect backup coverage
Owner: Gaurav
System: PostgreSQL recovery
Status: draft
Check which datasets and configurations are covered, latest scheduled job outcome, retention, permitted storage location and failure alerts. Ask the database team to confirm the actual schedule and protection of recovery material.
Compare a successful job with a separately documented isolated restore. Do not treat an inventory screenshot or job status as recoverability proof.
Missing: retention approval, recent usable restore record, key-access approval and agreed RTO/RPO.
Impact: a backup can exist while recovery remains blocked by permission, corruption or missing dependencies.
Sources: INC-04, INC-05 and document 14. Next action: TASK-06, TASK-14 and TASK-15.
Escalation: database owner and security/IAM owner. Never copy secret values into this platform.

## Procedure: PostgreSQL recovery - plan an isolated restore
Owner: Gaurav
System: PostgreSQL recovery
Status: draft
Meaning: demonstrate recoverability without overwriting the live database.
1. Obtain exercise approval, a named database supervisor and an isolated target with no production routing.
2. Confirm dataset permission, selected recovery point, storage/key access and cleanup responsibility.
3. Ask an authorised database operator to follow the reviewed restore procedure in that target.
4. Record start/end observations, integrity checks, expected sample counts and application compatibility checks.
5. Review missing or duplicate orders and payment reconciliation implications.
6. Store a sanitised result and reviewer assessment. If blocked, record the blocker instead of a pass.
Stop on a production target, unapproved personal/customer data, missing key permission or unknown backup provenance.
Missing: approved target, usable backup evidence, supervisor and actual execution results.
Sources: documents 13 and 22; exercise EX-06 in document 30.
Next action: TASK-15. No restore has been executed by this case-study import.

knowledge.title: ShopEase customer journey
knowledge.summary:
## Architecture: ShopEase customer journey
System: ShopEase
Status: current draft
Customers reach the Web storefront, which calls the API service. The API writes orders to PostgreSQL and sends payment requests to Payment provider. Payment callbacks are processed by the Payment worker. GitHub Actions builds Docker packages for the proposed AWS ECS deployment. CloudWatch holds operational logs and alerts.
Meaning: a working home page does not prove orders and payments are consistent.
Missing information: exact cloud resource identifiers and approved production inventory are not supplied.
Next action: compare this map with authorised infrastructure inventory before approving it.
